figures.title: The OIBOK working model
figures.summary: Three recurring transformations, six capabilities and the connections that support organisational response.
reading: Orient brings relevant signals and knowledge into an understanding of the situation. Sense and Know are its two capabilities.
Coordinate connects authorised commitment and collective response through Choose and Mobilise.
Improve uses evaluated consequences to revise understanding and capability through Learn and Adapt.
Contextualise is a connective mechanism and organisational orientation is an integrated state. They are not additional capabilities.
Memory supplies continuity across the work. Purpose, governance and responsible exercise span every capability. Feedback can return to both Orient and Coordinate.
figures.boundary: The transformations overlap and recur. The six capabilities have equal status. AI participation is optional. The model is a literature-grounded working synthesis, with independent field validation pending.

figures.title: Applying OIBOK to one real problem
figures.summary: Connect investigation, work design, evaluation and retained learning around one bounded piece of work.
reading: Define the work, desired outcome, affected people, boundary and decision owner.
Follow contrasting cases using the Practice Review. Expand its Context and Knowledge Map and Decision and Coordination Canvas where the evidence warrants it.
Compare current practice, a credible non-AI improvement and any specific AI contribution. Further inquiry or retaining current practice are legitimate decisions.
Use the AI canvas when an AI option proceeds into design. Prepare the Outcome and Learning Record before trying the selected change.
Review consequences and competing explanations, record the next decision and embed useful learning in later work. Revisit the problem or design whenever the evidence warrants it.
figures.boundary: This is a reading and practice aid, not a compulsory sequence of gates. Records can develop together. A non-AI change still needs authority, evaluation and later learning.

figures.title: From handoff to accepted commitment
figures.summary: A fictional Linden Studio example of acceptance, clarification, ownership and verified effects.
reading: The client lead prepares the brief with scope, requested timing, dependencies and available evidence.
The delivery lead checks scope, dependencies and capacity before accepting delivery responsibility. A submitted brief does not itself confirm the commitment.
If clarification is needed, the client lead retains responsibility for correction and resubmission in this fictional arrangement. Exceptions requiring authority go to the owner.
After acceptance and required authorisation, a date can be confirmed and the work carried through. Performance and verified effects remain distinct.
An uncertain action result requires checking the real state before repeating or reversing an action. Keep unresolved work visibly owned.
figures.boundary: Linden Studio is wholly fictional. Its proposed change has no recorded implementation, measured benefit or persistence result. General OIBOK guidance requires an agreed owner while a handoff is waiting or disputed; it does not mandate the same owner in every organisation.

figures.title: People AI and authority in one workflow
figures.summary: A fictional Harbour Services arrangement for source-linked drafting, review, escalation and fallback.
reading: The policy owner maintains the governing source, current version and route for resolving ambiguity.
AI retrieves approved material and prepares a draft. Its technical ability creates no permission to decide or act.
A named adviser checks the source, version, context and proposed response within their authority. Meaningful review needs evidence, expertise, time and power to reject or stop.
Missing or conflicting policy requires abstention and escalation. Excluded cases leave the standard workflow. The established manual process is the fallback.
An authorised person approves the external reply and records what happened. In this example AI cannot send replies, approve refunds, change policy or act externally.
figures.boundary: This is the fictional Harbour configuration, not a universal prohibition on authorised AI actions in other settings. Proposed controls require evidence that they operate as intended.

figures.title: Evaluating the change and AI contribution
figures.summary: Compare complete working arrangements and keep alternative explanations visible.
reading: Arrangement A is current practice. Arrangement B is an improved working arrangement without AI. Arrangement C adds AI to the same improved arrangement.
A comparison of A and C examines the complete package. A comparison of B and C is relevant to the additional contribution of AI.
Use comparable definitions and observation periods. Assess beneficiary outcomes, quality, total effort, safeguards and whether the intended arrangement was used.
Consider case mix, workload, extra expert support, staff learning, concurrent changes and measurement changes as possible explanations.
Attach the conclusion to the tested setting, people, cases, period and configuration. Record the accountable decision to continue, adapt, stop or defer.
figures.boundary: A three-column comparison is not itself a causal evaluation design. Selection, allocation, missing outcomes and other design features determine what the evidence supports. A local workflow result does not establish organisation-wide intelligence.

figures.title: From a lesson to lasting capability
figures.summary: Connect evaluated experience to changed work and later evidence of usable organisational capability.
reading: Form a challengeable lesson from evaluated experience, with supporting evidence, uncertainty and conditions of applicability.
Translate it into working arrangements: guidance, decision rights, handoffs, system configuration, expertise or resources. Assign owners and completion evidence.
Place current knowledge where the next relevant decision can use it. Preserve source, scope, version, review condition and supersession.
Examine later reuse, another suitably prepared person doing the work, and relevant changed conditions. Choose safe cases or rehearsals when needed.
Retain, revise or retire arrangements in light of the evidence. Separate a completed action from capability demonstrated over the horizon of the claim.
figures.boundary: The three practical checks are proposed inquiry prompts, not a validated score or universal measurement threshold. A planned check remains planned until evidence is recorded. Continuity can include explicit ongoing dependencies.

figures.title: A shared vocabulary for one workflow
figures.summary: An illustrative relationship map connecting evidence, policy, expertise, authority, decisions and action.
reading: A case or request provides the work and purpose that the decision concerns.
Evidence supports the decision, while a policy version governs it under stated conditions. Retain provenance, currentness and uncertainty.
Relevant expertise informs the interpretation. An authorised role may commit the organisation within stated limits. These are different relationships even when one person holds both roles.
The decision permits specified action. The work state records completion, dependency, exception or an uncertain result.
Test the vocabulary against contrasting real cases, assign ownership and preserve meaningful differences. A glossary or linked table can support the same inquiry.
figures.boundary: This is an illustrative local representation, not a canonical or validated OIBOK ontology. A graph database is optional. The relationships must be checked against the work and its actual authority.

figures.title: One inquiry across the OIBOK tools
figures.summary: A fictional Harbour Services case showing what carries forward between working records.
reading: Case HS-01 connects Practice Review PR-HS-01, AI design AI-HS-01 and Outcome and Learning Record OL-HS-01.
The review carries forward the problem, boundary, sources, competing explanations and knowledge or authority gaps. Its two supporting maps remain linked to that inquiry.
The work design carries the complete intervention, eligible cases, exclusions, comparison, measures, permissions and stop rules into evaluation.
The results record carries observations, missing outcomes, limitations, the decision, corrective actions and the later review into continuing practice.
The receiving owner checks usable evidence, permitted next action and unresolved conditions. Records can develop together; suitable existing organisational records can be reused.
figures.boundary: The case is fictional. Its adapt-and-extend decision is conditional on corrections, retesting and named reviewers. Follow-up action completion is not yet recorded and the week-eight persistence check remains pending.

figures.title: How review effort changes the resource case
figures.summary: Fictional Wattle Supply assumptions show why total work matters when comparing an AI option.
reading: The comparison assumes 240 eligible catalogue entries per month. Preparation, review and correction minutes are converted to staff hours, then monthly maintenance is added.
Current practice totals 50 staff hours. The non-AI improvement totals 39. Adding AI with three-minute review totals 29. Increasing AI review to six minutes totals 41.
The AI option includes the non-AI improvements. Its setup is 30 staff hours in total, compared with 10 for the non-AI improvement, and it adds AUD 120 in monthly cash charges.
The difference represents potential released capacity, not an assumed payroll saving. Accuracy, quality, turnaround and redeployability still need evaluation.
Replace the assumptions with actual case evidence before authorising a material decision. Preserve original assumptions so later findings can challenge them.
figures.boundary: All volumes, times and charges are invented teaching inputs. There are no observed results. Setup effort, recurring staff-time value and cash expenditure are separate quantities.
